items.headline: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
items.blurb: The BBC joins Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi as it regains crucial territory in the Donbas, but optimism has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump.
items.text: A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker. Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back. This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control. While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. items.headline: Oregon school shooter was former special needs student, police say
items.blurb: A teacher fought teenage shooter and a parent shot him dead, police say on Friday, a day after four people were killed.
items.text: The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon was a former special-needs student at the school, police and school officials have said. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the attacker on Friday, a day after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, as Griffin J. John II. He said the teenager attacked a classroom of special-needs students, where all the victims were shot. Steven Cook, superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools, said John was not enrolled in the local public school system at the time. “That classroom was a special needs classroom, and the suspect was a special needs student in that school,” Cook told a news conference. Krantz said John shot his way through locked doors with a 12-gauge shotgun, firing as many as 15 shots, and had about 44 rounds left when he was killed. items.headline: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
items.blurb: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report .
items.text: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report . More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status. The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years. The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations. items.headline: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
items.blurb: The 16-year-old suspect previously attended the primary school and had targeted a special educational needs classroom, police say.
items.text: An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class. As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander armed with a pistol ran inside and killed the teen. The bystander, a father of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend on Thursday lunchtime when he saw the suspect firing in the car park, then shooting through a window to enter. Police said the 16-year-old suspect used to be a student at the school. Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class. items.text: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.” Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho. items.headline: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
items.blurb: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.
items.text: Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt. Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence : a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby. The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car. "We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head and my neck – look, I am bleeding!" items.headline: Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
items.blurb: Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions
items.text: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign. Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions. “This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”. Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”. Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks. The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported. items.text: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday. The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr , secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist. Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week. items.headline: Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
items.blurb: Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.
items.text: Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax. Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider". Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters. She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job. Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One. "I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said. "You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media. The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job

items.text: The number of patients opting outpatient and diagnostic services at Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) in Hyderabad has risen in the past one month. File | Photo Credit: NAGARA GOPAL The Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) in Hyderabad has witnessed a rise in patient footfall over the past month, with more than 5,000 patients accessing various services at the hospital daily. According to statistics shared by the hospital, NIMS recorded 5,635 outpatient (OP) patients in a single day recently — the highest daily OP attendance recorded in the recent period. The hospital had earlier received around 3,500 OP patients a day. The Diagnostics and Investigations Department also recorded a high volume of patients, with 5,088 people undergoing various investigations in a single day. As many as 306 patients were admitted as inpatients (IP) on the same day. The Emergency Department too witnessed an increase in admissions. items.headline: Apex court stays Bhopal trial in Twisha death case
items.blurb: The petition was filed by Twisha’s father, who cited concerns over a fair trial in Bhopal and sought proceedings to be moved to Delhi.
items.text: The Supreme Court on Friday stayed the trial in the unnatural death case of former model and actor Twisha Sharma in Bhopal and issued notices to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) , her husband Samarth Singh and mother-in-law Giribala Singh on a plea seeking transfer of the proceedings to Delhi. A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi passed the order on a petition filed by Twisha’s father, Navnidhi Sharma, who expressed apprehension that his daughter would not receive a fair trial in Madhya Pradesh because of the influence wielded by her mother-in-law, a retired district judge. Navnidhi’s lawyers told the court that he sought the transfer as he was based in the Delhi-NCR region. The case is pending before an additional district and sessions judge in Bhopal. The Supreme Court had taken suo motu cognisance of Twisha’s death in May amid concerns over the fairness of the investigation by the Madhya Pradesh Police . The probe was subsequently transferred to the CBI. Twisha, 33, was found hanging at her matrimonial home in Bhopal

items.blurb: Keralam government orders the suspension citing likelihood of severe traffic congestion as construction work remains incomplete
items.text: National Highway 66 in Keralam. (File photo) | Photo Credit: The Hindu The Keralam government on Thursday ordered the suspension of toll collection on national highway (NH) 66 at Nattika in Thrissur, citing the likelihood of severe traffic congestion as construction work remains incomplete. The decision followed reports from the District Collector and the police that starting toll collection before the completion of the Kodungallur-Kaprikkad stretch could disrupt traffic and cause considerable inconvenience to commuters. Several works, including the service road on the Kodungallur-Kaprikkad section and the approach roads to bridges, are yet to be completed. Public Works Minister P.K. Basheer directed the District Collector to convene a meeting with police officials, people’s representatives and officials of the departments concerned to assess the situation and take an appropriate decision. He also instructed the Collector to inspect the site and submit a detailed report. A decision on commencing toll collection will be taken only after the pending road works are completed and smooth and safe traffic movement is ensured, the Minister assured. Giaspura had allegedly told the media outside the secretariat, located in the Darbar Sahib complex, that he faced caste-based discrimination. The statement said A legislators appeared at the secretariat on Friday in compliance with directions issued by the Jathedar Akal Takht Sahib. They admitted their mistake, acknowledging that despite the Jathedar's directions, they had neither contradicted Giaspura's allegations before the media on October 12 nor clarified that they had not faced any caste-based discrimination and that Giaspura had made inappropriate remarks, it said. items.headline: Florida art dealer gets nearly 4 years in prison for scheme to sell fake Andy Warhol artworks
items.blurb: Florida art dealer gets nearly 4 years in prison for scheme to sell fake Andy Warhol artworks
items.text: MIAMI (AP) — A South Florida art dealer has been sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison for a scheme that involved selling fake Andy Warhol artworks. Leslie Howard Roberts, 63, was sentenced in Miami federal court this month to three years and 10 months after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. He must also pay back nearly $2.6 million that he earned from the scheme. Roberts, the owner of Miami Fine Art Gallery in Coconut Grove, was arrested in April 2025 . According to court records, he fraudulently represented art as original pieces created by renowned artist Andy Warhol. Prosecutors said Roberts falsely claimed that he acquired the artwork directly from the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts and provided fake and fraudulent invoices. “He exploited the trust that collectors place in art dealers and the authenticity of the works they purchase,” U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones said in a statement. items.blurb: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries rose in August from the lowest level since October 2025, led by increases in the stockpiles of Canada and Belgium.
items.text: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries rose in August from the lowest level since October 2025, led by increases in the stockpiles of Canada and Belgium. Overseas holdings climbed more than $83 billion from July, according to data published by the Treasury Department on Friday. The total now stands at $9.33 trillion. The foreign holdings data incorporate changes in valuation as well as net sales and purchases. The Bloomberg US Treasury index advanced 0.3% in August, before a tumble in September on concerns about persistent inflation and a new cycle of Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes. Japan, the biggest foreign holder of Treasuries, saw a $36 billion drop in its holdings, to $1.1 trillion, the lowest since December 2024. Japanese officials were intervening over the summer in the foreign-exchange market, buying yen amid a slump in the currency to its weakest in four decades against the dollar. Japanese data last month suggested Tokyo sold a portion of its holdings of Treasuries and other securities. items.headline: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
items.blurb: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
items.text: Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC. Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time. The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes. The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode". Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%. Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

items.headline: Compass Files Suit Over California Home Listing Service Rules
items.blurb: Compass Inc., the top US broker for residential properties, sued California’s largest real estate listing service in the latest escalation of a broader legal fight over timely access to information about homes for sale.
items.text: (Bloomberg) -- Compass Inc., the top US broker for residential properties, sued California’s largest real estate listing service in the latest escalation of a broader legal fight over timely access to information about homes for sale. The federal court suit filed Friday in Los Angeles accuses the California Regional Multiple Listing Service, or CRMLS, of adopting anticompetitive rules. Compass alleged the requirement that agents list homes for sale within one business day or face fines violates US antitrust laws. CRMLS covers 22 counties in the state, including areas around Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area and San Diego. The legal battle pits Compass’ effort to build a private listing network against the decades-old industry practice of relying on multiple listing services across the country. “Homeowners should be free to choose how to sell their own homes without having a competition-killing real estate industry organization tell them how to do it,” Compass said in the complaint. items.blurb: Sixteen years since FirstCry began its journey, what began as a kidswear marketplace has spawned a massive multi-channel ecommerce and…
items.text: FirstCry's Q1FY27 consolidated revenue rose 13.1% YoY to ₹2,106.2 Cr, while net loss narrowed 34% to ₹44 Cr. India multichannel grew 17.7%, but GlobalBees revenue was largely flat. As quick-commerce competition intensifies, FirstCry is expanding faster delivery while managing store costs, GlobalBees' slowdown and its loss-making international business.
